title: Brand Delivered, and Quality That Holds
subtitle: A design system that carries the brand into the product, and a build that refuses work which has left it

bio.short: Head of Product Design at Bibel TV, where the design system across iOS, Android, web and connected TV is mine. Brand reaches the product through it, and the build refuses work that has left it.
bio.long:
I am Head of Product Design at Bibel TV. In each of my last three roles the design system was mine to own. Datameer, then Ninox, and now Bibel TV, where the last year has gone almost entirely into it.

You describe Oxygen as two things in one sentence. It is how the brand reaches the product. It is also the infrastructure that keeps quality from drifting once interfaces are generated rather than drawn. I have spent the last year building both, hands-on.

The brand half is a color engine. Bibel TV has more than ten thousand videos in its catalog. No one can hand-pick a theme for each, so the theme is computed from the artwork itself. I built it in OKLCH rather than RGB. Every card then carries an evenly weighted theme, and a grid of them reads as one surface. WCAG contrast is validated inside the algorithm, so no theme can ship failing it. The engine is live in production, with the tool that tunes its thresholds. That is brand consistency computed rather than policed.

The quality half sits above the tokens. Storybook is the source of truth rather than a Figma file, with a prototyping layer on top. The people who build with this system are product managers and external engineers, not designers. The token vocabulary is handed to an AI assistant as an enumerated list rather than recalled. The compliant path is then also the fastest one. Checks run identically on a laptop and in CI. They refuse a token reference that does not resolve, or a color written straight into a component. Neither of those is a visible difference, so the build is the only reviewer that reliably catches them. Design authority in an organization without designers lives in whatever the build refuses. Everything else is advice.

Underneath both is the token architecture, and it is not the one a textbook would draw. Four tiers: primitives, semantic, component, and page or view. The top two add no new values at all. They alias downward, and that redundancy is the point. Each is a place the company can change spacing, type size or radius itself, without waiting on the agency that owns the code. It is also the first step toward server-driven UI for the streaming part of the app. The part I find most telling is that the agency backed it. The architecture takes billable change work away from them, and they were enthusiastic anyway.

Governance is the same instinct one layer higher. At Ninox the design system was mine, and I built joint governance with engineering around it. It ran as a working group with an assigned design lead and an assigned engineering lead. It had a meeting rhythm, and a documented process for identifying component changes and escalating them to the group. At Bibel TV the exception mechanism does that job. Anything off-system has to be annotated with a reason and recorded. The build fails until that record is updated. So the register of exceptions doubles as an honest roadmap of what the system still needs, written by whoever hit the friction.

Accessibility and multi-market constraints run through all of it. At ChurchDesk we audited our own website, and also the websites customers build with the platform, for EU Accessibility Act compliance. The second half is the harder one. Those sites are made by parish staff rather than by specialists, so the standard has to hold in output nobody trained for. Those same customers were then given a legal accessibility deadline of their own, and almost none of them have anyone technical. I shipped the capability that met it for them automatically, across six countries, under GDPR plus Protestant and Catholic church data-protection law. Screen-reader semantics and ARIA are standing practice for me. Before that came five years at Datameer, on an analytics platform for top US, Canadian and UK banks and insurers. It operated under HIPAA among other frameworks.

I would not hand the Bibel TV architecture to Doctolib unchanged. It answers one company's constraints, and yours are different. Many product teams, multiple markets, and a brand that has to hold across all of them. What travels is the habit of deriving the system from the organization rather than from the canon. And the habit of being able to say what each decision costs.

context.emphasis: Lead with both halves of the posting's own definition of Oxygen, in the posting's order. First the brand. The color engine computes themes from content artwork in OKLCH, with WCAG contrast validated inside the algorithm. That is brand consistency computed rather than policed, and it is live. Then the quality layer. Storybook is the source of truth, the token vocabulary is handed to an assistant as an enumerated list, and CI refuses off-system work. Those are requirements 4 and 13, which most applicants will answer with a philosophy rather than a mechanism. Then the token architecture as a control surface, derived from how the organization works rather than from the canon. That judgment is what transfers to a system serving many teams and markets. Then governance and contribution: the Ninox working group, and the Bibel TV exception register. Then the regulated, multi-market, accessible record, which is requirements 8 and 9. The leadership record sits behind all of it so the Head-of seat reads as credible. It is never a separate pitch. See data/applications/doctolib-head-of-design-system/positioning.md. If this page argues something that file does not, one of the two is wrong.
